Clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, First Contact Practitioner, HCPC PH128483. Last updated: June 2026.

Quick answer: Joint replacement surgery is considered when severe, persistent pain affects daily activities and sleep, other treatments have failed, X-rays show significant joint damage, and quality of life is impacted. In the UK, over 200,000 hip and knee replacements occur annually, and more than 90% of people report significant improvement in pain and mobility.

Joint replacement surgery sounds daunting. It is natural to feel anxious — but it is also one of the most successful operations in modern medicine. In the UK, more than 200,000 hip and knee replacements are performed each year, and over 90% of people report significant improvement in pain and mobility.

This guide explains everything in plain English, from deciding if surgery is right for you to what recovery actually feels like.

When Is Joint Replacement the Right Choice?

Joint replacement is not the first option. You and your doctor will usually consider it when you have severe persistent pain affecting your sleep and daily activities, other treatments have not provided enough relief, X-rays show significant joint damage, and your quality of life is being seriously affected. It is a decision you make with your orthopaedic surgeon, not one they make for you.

Knee Replacement Surgery — What to Expect

A total knee replacement (knee arthroplasty) involves removing the damaged surfaces of the knee joint and replacing them with metal and plastic implants. The operation takes about 1–2 hours, usually under spinal anaesthetic or general anaesthetic. You will typically stay in hospital for 1–3 days. You will be encouraged to stand and take a few steps with a walking frame within 24 hours, and a physiotherapist will guide you through the first exercises. Most people notice improved mobility within 6–12 weeks, with continued gains for up to a year.

Hip Replacement Surgery — Recovery and Results

Hip replacements follow a similar pattern to knee replacements. The damaged ball-and-socket joint is replaced with artificial components. Hip replacement generally has a slightly quicker early recovery than knee replacement. Many people go home within 1–2 days. Use crutches or a walking frame for 2–6 weeks, follow hip precautions if advised, and most people can drive after about 6 weeks (check with your insurance provider). You may return to work within 6–12 weeks depending on your job.

Getting on the NHS Waiting List

The pathway typically involves GP referral to an orthopaedic consultant, specialist assessment with X-ray review, decision to proceed, pre-operative assessment (blood tests, heart tracing, health checks), and finally a surgery date. The NHS Constitution target is a maximum of 18 weeks from referral to treatment, but waits may be longer in some areas.

Preparing for Surgery (Pre-habilitation)

What you do before surgery significantly affects how well you recover after. Strengthen your muscles around the joint — stronger muscles mean faster recovery. Maintain a healthy weight — excess weight puts extra stress on your new joint and increases surgical risks. Stop smoking — it slows healing and raises complication risks. Eat well, and plan your home: arrange help with shopping, cooking, and transport for the first few weeks, and clear trip hazards.

Recovery Timeline and Rehabilitation

Everyone recovers at their own pace. Week 1–2: walking with a frame or crutches inside the house, daily physio exercises, swelling and discomfort peak then improve. Weeks 2–6: gradually reduce walking aids, start walking outside, continue exercises. Weeks 6–12: walking freely, return to driving, may return to office-based work. 3–6 months: significant improvement in pain and function. 6–12 months: continued gains, resume low-impact sports. Knee replacements tend to have a slightly slower recovery than hips.

Life After Joint Replacement

The goal is a life with less pain and more movement. Most people can walk without pain, sleep through the night, return to hobbies like gardening and swimming, and travel comfortably. You should avoid high-impact activities like running or jumping. Modern implants often last 15–25 years or more.

Alternatives to Surgery

Surgery is not the only way forward. Some people manage well with weight loss (even 5–10% of body weight can significantly reduce knee pain), a tailored physiotherapy exercise programme, a pain management programme combining physical and psychological strategies, walking aids and supports, or steroid injections for temporary relief. Always explore these with your GP or physiotherapist first.

Practical next steps for Joint Replacement Surgery for Arthritis — A Complete UK Guide

If you came here about Joint Replacement Surgery for Arthritis — A Complete UK Guide, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Supplements versus meals

Food-first is usually safer than stacking capsules. If you do try a supplement, choose a reputable UK brand, check for interactions with your medicines (especially blood thinners), and give any trial a clear stop date so you can judge whether symptoms truly changed.

Quick questions about Joint Replacement Surgery Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
